newsitem.title: FRANCE: France ready to share Nazi gold among victims.
newsitem.headline: France ready to share Nazi gold among victims.

text.p: Saying President Jacques Chirac valued morality more than legality, French officials said on Thursday Paris agreed that Nazi gold still held by World War Two allies could go to Hitler's victims.

"Yes, we agree the gold can eventually go to the victims," a Chirac spokesman said after presidential aide Jean-David Levitte received Rabbi Abraham Cooper, associate dean of the Simon Weisenthal Centre at the Elysee presidential palace.

"I believe we have an ally in President Chirac," said Cooper, who came from his Nazi-hunting group's U.S. headquarters to seek backing for plans to share the last 5.5 tonnes of gold jointly held by the United States, Britain and France among war victims.

It has been stored in London and New York since 1946 but French officials said two tonnes were scheduled to come to France. "He (Levitte) said it could be earmarked for victims' claims but London and Washington must also agree," Cooper said.
The gold is all that remains of 377 tonnes looted by the Nazis, recovered at the end of the war and since re-distributed by a Tripartite Gold Commission (TGC).
Current TGC policy is to distribute gold among states, excluding individual victims, in what Cooper calls "a major rip-off".

"Some gold came from national banks looted by the Nazis. But much was from victims -- privately held gold, jewellry, wedding bands and, yes, gold teeth the Nazis wrenched from the mouths of their victims after gassing them to death," he told Reuters.

The Weisenthal Centre has asked Washington, London and Paris to change TGC policy and share out the 5.5 tonnes, primarily among ageing concentration camp survivors whatever their nationality or religion.
"This is not charity. This is a matter of reassigning property that people really owned," he said.
Cooper said British Foreign Office Permanent Undersecretary of State Liam Fox told him in London last week he could count on Britain's support.

"We have still not heard from President Clinton but we can now tell him we have the backing of two out of three. President Chirac's aides told us they fully agreed this was an urgent matter because the clock is ticking and the last survivors are aged," Cooper said.

Nazi loot is also an issue in France where Prime Minister Alain Juppe told Jewish leaders on Saturday he would set up a commission to clarify the status of property never returned to its rightful owners after the war, mostly because they were killed in gas chambers.
A recent book said French authorities took over from the retreating Germans in 1944, and still administered, possibly hundreds of flats left vacant by Jews killed in death camps.
A government body also determined that nearly 2,000 works of art, possibly seized from Jews, were still "provisionally" in care of French museums more than 50 years after the war.

Juppe's announcement also followed moves to shed light on the dark years of World War Two in other countries including neutral Switzerland and Sweden, which both have been accused of profitably dealing with the Nazis and being paid in gold seized from their victims.
